title: Pauri 22, sound: paataalaa paataal

segments.voice: Yesterday, the hour creation began. Your line was only the maker knows. Did you say I don't know, once, and let it be fine? Today, from when to where. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

Stand in an elevator in a very tall building and look at the buttons. Basement, sub-basement, parking level three. And above you, floor after floor, up to a number you can barely read. Now imagine the buttons never end, in either direction. Below the lowest basement, another. Above the top floor, another sky. Yesterday Japji asked when. Today it asks where, and how far. And the first line of Pauri 22 sounds like that endless elevator.
screen: `AN ELEVATOR, BASEMENT TO SKY.` → `THE BUTTONS NEVER END.` → `FROM WHEN TO WHERE.`

segments.voice: Here's the first line of Pauri 22, in the original: paataalaa paataal lakh aagaasaa aagaas. Let's take it apart. Paataal, paa-TAAL: the lower worlds, the regions under the earth. In old Indian cosmology, there were said to be many of them, one below another. Paataalaa paataal: underworlds below underworlds. Lakh: a hundred thousand, the word Indians still use for big numbers, as in five lakh rupees. Aagaas, aa-GAAS: sky, the heavens, related to the Sanskrit akasha. Aagaasaa aagaas: skies beyond skies. So: underworlds below underworlds, and hundreds of thousands of skies above skies. Now listen to how it's built. Each half doubles its word: paataalaa paataal, aagaasaa aagaas. The first form of the word, with the extra aa, reaches, and the second one lands. It sounds like going down a staircase, step after step, and then climbing into the sky, step after step. The line doesn't describe the size of the universe. It lets the mouth do the measuring. It also carries on what the countless stanzas started, but now in a direction. Asankh was about number. This is about depth and height: down, down, up, up. The rest of the stanza will ask whether anyone has found the end, and whether it could ever be written. That's tomorrow. Today, just the elevator, and the sound of it: paataalaa paataal.
screen: `PAATAAL — THE LOWER WORLDS.` · `LAKH — A HUNDRED THOUSAND.` · `AAGAAS — SKY, SKIES BEYOND SKIES.` · `DOWN, DOWN, UP, UP.` · then, large: `PAATAALAA PAATAAL.`

segments.voice: Say the first line aloud: paataalaa paataal, lakh aagaasaa aagaas. On the first half, let your attention sink down, into your seat, into the floor, into the ground beneath. On the second half, let it rise, to the crown of your head and the space above it. Say it twice more. Then sit quietly between the two, the ground below and the open space above. The bell holds the time.
Pauri 22. It opens paataalaa paataal, lakh aagaasaa aagaas: underworlds below underworlds, hundreds of thousands of skies above skies.
Your line: paataalaa paataal. Today, when you ride an elevator or climb stairs, let the line play, and imagine the steps never ending. Day one hundred ninety-seven.

screen: `DAY 197 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: PAURI 22, MEANING: WORLDS BEYOND WORLDS.`

howItsDone: Pauri 22 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; its opening line, with its doubled words, has a rhythm that can be heard even before the meaning.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old map of heaven and hell.
what it means: creation goes on in every direction, deeper and higher than anyone can reach.
what a scholar hears: paataal is related to Sanskrit patala, the lower regions, and aagaas to akasha, sky; the doubled forms make the line feel like endless steps.
